title: Mononuclear IUPAC Nomenclature Rules & Oxidation State Rules
topics: Mononuclear Complex IUPAC Architecture: [Cation] ──► [Ligands in Alphabetical Order] ──► [Metal] ──► [(Oxidation State)]
Ligand Suffix Conventions (-ido for anionic ligands, standard/special names for neutral ligands: aqua, ammine, carbonyl, nitrosyl)
Multiplicity Prefixes: Simple (di-, tri-, tetra-) vs Complex (bis-, tris-, tetrakis-)
Central Metal Naming: Standard name in cationic/neutral vs -ate suffix in anionic complexes (ferrate, cuprate, plumbate, argentate, aurate, stannate)
quickSummary: IUPAC Naming: Cation named first, then ligands in strict alphabetical order, then central metal with Roman numeral oxidation state in parentheses without space. In anionic complexes, metal ends in -ate. Neutral ligands: aqua (H₂O), ammine (NH₃), carbonyl (CO), nitrosyl (NO).
summary: Master IUPAC naming rules for coordination compounds, alphabetical ligand conventions, metal suffixes, and oxidation state calculations.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
MONONUCLEAR COMPLEX IUPAC NAMING
                      
   [ Cation Name ] ──► [ Ligands in Alphabetical Order ] ──► [ Metal Name ] ──► [ (Oxidation State) ]
conceptBreakdown.content:
1. **Naming Order**: The cation is named first, followed by the anion, regardless of whether the complex ion is cationic or anionic.
2. **Ligand Naming**: Ligands are named in strict alphabetical order before the central metal.
   - **Anionic Ligands**: End in *-ido* (e.g., $\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow$ chlorido, $\text{CN}^- \rightarrow$ cyanido, $\text{OH}^- \rightarrow$ hydroxido, $\text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow$ oxido, $\text{ox}^{2-} \rightarrow$ oxalato).
   - **Neutral Ligands**: Retain molecular names (Exceptions: $\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow$ aqua, $\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow$ ammine, $\text{CO} \rightarrow$ carbonyl, $\text{NO} \rightarrow$ nitrosyl).
   - **Prefixes for Multiplicity**: Use *di-, tri-, tetra-* for simple ligands; use *bis-, tris-, tetrakis-* for complex ligands containing numerical prefixes (e.g., ethylenediamine $\rightarrow$ bis(ethane-1,2-diamine)).
3. **Central Metal Suffix**:
   - *Cationic or Neutral Complexes*: Metal retains standard English name (Cobalt, Iron, Copper).
   - *Anionic Complexes*: Metal ends in **-ate** ($\text{Fe} \rightarrow$ ferrate, $\text{Cu} \rightarrow$ cuprate, $\text{Pb} \rightarrow$ plumbate, $\text{Ag} \rightarrow$ argentate, $\text{Au} \rightarrow$ aurate, $\text{Sn} \rightarrow$ stannate).
4. **Oxidation State**: Indicated by a Roman numeral in parentheses immediately following the metal name without a space.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
IUPAC EXAMPLES
                      
   $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_5(\text{CO}_3)]\text{Cl}$  ──► Pentaamminecarbonatocobalt(III) chloride
   $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$        ──► Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III)
   $[\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl(NH}_2\text{CH}_3)]\text{Cl}$ ──► Diamminechlorido(methanamine)platinum(II) chloride
   $[\text{Cr(H}_2\text{O})_4\text{Cl}_2]^+$    ──► Tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) ion
   $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$        ──► Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II)
   $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$           ──► Tetracarbonylnickel(0)
conceptBreakdown.content: Review the precise spelling, alphabetical priority, and oxidation states in standard IUPAC coordination nomenclature.

quickRevision: Cation is named first, then anion.
Ligands in alphabetical order, irrespective of charge.
Anionic ligands end in -ido (chlorido, cyanido, hydroxido).
Neutral ligand exceptions: aqua (H₂O), ammine (NH₃), carbonyl (CO), nitrosyl (NO).
Anionic complex metal name takes -ate suffix (ferrate, cuprate, argentate).
Roman numeral oxidation state in parentheses with no space.
